facts.title: The Sun Is a Working Star
facts.body: The Sun is a medium-sized star at the center of the solar system. It produces energy through nuclear fusion in its core. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.

facts.title: The Moon Guides Tides and Time
facts.body:
The Moon is Earth’s natural satellite. Its gravity is the main cause of ocean tides. The same side always faces Earth because of tidal locking.

Moon phases depend on the changing angle between the Sun, Earth, and Moon. Its surface preserves impact craters for long ages.

facts.title: Mercury’s Fast and Harsh World
facts.body:
Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. It has almost no thick atmosphere to hold heat. A Mercurian day and year create unusual cycles of daylight.

Its surface is heavily cratered like the Moon. Spacecraft studies revealed water ice in shadowed polar craters.

facts.title: Venus Wrapped in Clouds
facts.body:
Venus is similar in size to Earth but very different in conditions. Its thick atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide. A runaway greenhouse effect makes its surface extremely hot.

Venus rotates very slowly and in the opposite direction of most planets. Clouds of sulfuric acid hide much of the surface from ordinary view.

facts.title: Earth the Water World
facts.body:
Earth is the only known planet with stable liquid water on its surface. Its atmosphere and magnetic field help protect life. Plate tectonics reshapes the surface over time.

The planet’s climate system links oceans, air, ice, and living things. Earth orbits in a region where temperatures can support liquid water.

facts.title: Mars and the Search for Ancient Water
facts.body:
Mars is a cold rocky planet often called the red planet. Iron-rich minerals give its soil a rusty color. Rovers and orbiters have found strong signs that liquid water existed there long ago.

Mars has enormous volcanoes and a vast canyon system. Scientists study Mars to learn whether it may once have supported microbial life.

facts.title: Jupiter the Giant with Many Moons
facts.body: Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system. It is mostly made of hydrogen and helium. Its Great Red Spot is a huge long-lived storm.

facts.title: Saturn and the Beauty of Rings
facts.body:
Saturn is a giant planet famous for its bright ring system. The rings are made mostly of ice particles mixed with rock and dust. Saturn is less dense than water on average.

Many moons orbit Saturn, including Titan and Enceladus. The planet’s winds and storms shape changing patterns in its atmosphere.

facts.title: Uranus Turns on Its Side
facts.body: Uranus is an ice giant with a blue-green appearance. Methane in its atmosphere helps give it that color. Its axis is tilted so extremely that the planet seems to roll around the Sun.

facts.title: Neptune and the Far Blue Winds
facts.body:
Neptune is the outermost major planet in the solar system. It is an ice giant with a deep blue color. Very fast winds move through its atmosphere.

Neptune was discovered through mathematical prediction before direct observation. Its moon Triton likely came from the distant outer regions of the solar system.

facts.title: Pluto and the Distant Icy Frontier
facts.body:
Pluto is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt. It has mountains of water ice and plains of frozen nitrogen. Its orbit is more tilted and stretched than those of the major planets.

Pluto and its large moon Charon orbit closely as a paired system. A spacecraft flyby revealed a surprisingly varied surface.

facts.title: Asteroids Left from Planet Building
facts.body:
Asteroids are rocky bodies left over from the early solar system. Many orbit in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. They range from tiny fragments to large objects hundreds of kilometers wide.

Some asteroids pass near Earth and are closely tracked. Studying them helps scientists understand planet formation.

facts.title: Comets with Tails of Dust and Gas
facts.body:
Comets are icy bodies that often come from the outer solar system. When they approach the Sun, heat releases gas and dust. That material can create glowing comas and long tails.

The tails point away from the Sun because of radiation and the solar wind. Comets preserve ancient material from the solar system’s early history.

facts.title: Meteors Across the Night Sky
facts.body:
A meteor is the streak of light made when a small space rock burns in the atmosphere. The object in space is called a meteoroid. If part of it reaches the ground, it becomes a meteorite.

Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through trails of debris. Many meteorites help scientists study material older than Earth’s surface rocks.

facts.title: The Milky Way as Our Galactic Home
facts.body:
The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains the Sun and solar system. It is a barred spiral galaxy with stars, gas, dust, and dark matter. From Earth, it appears as a pale band across a dark sky.

The solar system lies in one of its spiral arms. Studying the Milky Way helps astronomers place Earth in a much larger structure.

facts.title: Nebulae Where Stars Are Born
facts.body:
Nebulae are clouds of gas and dust in space. Some nebulae are regions where new stars form. Others are the remains of dying stars that have shed material.

Different gases glow in different colors when energized. Nebulae reveal how matter cycles through generations of stars.

facts.title: Black Holes and Extreme Gravity
facts.body:
A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape from within its event horizon. Most known black holes form after very massive stars collapse. Supermassive black holes sit in the centers of many galaxies.

Black holes can be detected by their effects on nearby matter and light. They are key test grounds for ideas about gravity and space.

facts.title: Stars Live Long Life Cycles
facts.body: Stars form from collapsing clouds of gas. They shine because fusion in their cores releases enormous energy. A star’s mass strongly affects its lifetime and fate. Some end as white dwarfs while the most massive may explode and leave neutron stars or black holes.

facts.title: Supernovae Seed the Cosmos
facts.body:
A supernova is a powerful stellar explosion. It can happen when a massive star dies or when a white dwarf becomes unstable. These explosions can briefly outshine entire galaxies.

Supernovae create and spread many heavy elements through space. They help trigger new rounds of star formation in nearby clouds.

facts.title: Exoplanets Beyond the Solar System
facts.body:
Exoplanets are planets orbiting stars other than the Sun. Thousands have been discovered using several detection methods. Some are giant hot worlds close to their stars, while others are small rocky planets.

Astronomers look for atmospheres and possible habitability clues. Exoplanet studies show that planetary systems are common and varied.

facts.title: The International Space Station in Orbit
facts.body: The International Space Station is a large laboratory that circles Earth. Astronauts live and work there in microgravity. Research on the station helps scientists study biology, physics, materials, and human health.

facts.title: Rockets Defy Earth’s Gravity
facts.body: Rockets work by pushing exhaust backward so the vehicle moves forward. This follows the conservation of momentum. Because rockets carry both fuel and oxidizer, they can work in space where there is no air.

facts.title: Satellites Above the Planet
facts.body: Artificial satellites orbit Earth and other worlds for many purposes. Some provide communication, navigation, and weather information. Others study climate, oceans, forests, and disasters from above. Different orbits are chosen depending on the mission.

facts.title: Auroras Paint the Polar Sky
facts.body:
Auroras are glowing displays seen near polar regions. They occur when charged particles from the Sun interact with Earth’s magnetic field and upper atmosphere. Different gases in the atmosphere can glow in different colors.

Auroras are linked to space weather and solar activity. They reveal that Earth is connected to events happening far out in space.

facts.title: Dark Matter and Cosmic Mystery
facts.body:
Dark matter is a form of matter inferred from gravity rather than direct light detection. It appears to make up much more of the universe’s matter than ordinary visible material. Galaxies rotate and cluster in ways that suggest dark matter is present.

Scientists still do not know its exact nature. Its mystery is one of the biggest open questions in astronomy.

facts.title: Exoplanets Are Common
facts.body: Astronomers have confirmed thousands of planets around other stars using transit dips and subtle stellar wobbles. Many systems look very different from our own solar system. Each discovery improves models of planet formation and helps narrow the search for potentially habitable worlds.

facts.title: Black Holes Shape Galaxies
facts.body: Supermassive black holes sit at the centers of most large galaxies. As matter falls in, energy released near the black hole can influence surrounding gas and star formation. So black holes are not only endpoints of gravity; they are also active drivers in galaxy evolution.
